newsitem.title: CANADA: Three senior executives quit at Arakis.
newsitem.headline: Three senior executives quit at Arakis.

text.p: Three of Arakis Energy Corp.'s top officers have resigned, trimming the company's executive ranks in a move it said Friday signalled a change in corporate direction.

Gone from Calgary, Alberta-based Arakis are vice presidents Peter Holstein, David Robinson and David Harrison, each of whom played a large role in the events leading up to Arakis' recent announcement of a $1 billion deal to develop its oil concessions in Sudan.
"I got a faxed resignation yesterday afternoon," Arakis Chief Executive Officer John McLeod said in an interview. "I knew things were not happy and we planned some changes in there as well."

McLeod said the resignations, as well as a share buyback also announced Friday, showed Arakis had become more of a legitimate oil company since the deal to develop the Sudan project with China National Petroleum Corp., Malaysia state oil company Petronas and the Sudan government was inked.
"The focus of the company changed when we signed this deal in Sudan," he said.
But one of the executives who quit said the resignations were fuelled by rifts over the membership of Arakis's board and the refusal to grant the trio more stock options for their work in 1996.

"We felt that there needed to be a number of independent outside directors brought into the company from within the oil industry and elsewhere," Robinson said, adding that the calls for an expanded board "were not taken seriously" by the company's management and current directors.

Among members of Arakis's four-director board are chairman Lutfur Khan, known for his connections with the Sudanese government, and McLeod, who was brought in to lead the company after the widely publicised collapse last year of a debt deal that would have financed the Sudan project.
Robinson said the perception remained that Arakis was still run by the same people who were at the helm "during last year's debacle," and that was pressuring its stock price.
He said the officials who resigned, especially Holstein, had played major roles in bringing in potential joint venture partners for the Sudan deal.

Arakis also said it would respond to recent shareholder calls by approving a share buyback. The company said the programme would give management discretion to buy up to 10 percent of Arakis' stock. The company said it had about $50 million and no immediate need for the cash.
Arakis shareholders, many of whom expected a big jump in the company's share price following the announcement of the long-awaited Sudan deal, were disappointed by the stock's lackluster showing.
Arakis stock took a rollercoaster ride Friday, tumbling as low as $2.50 and climbing to $3.63, before steadying at $3.25.
